slides.page_title: Why HTTP/1.1 Ran Out of Road

items: Methods, status codes, headers never changed across 1.1/2/3
RFC 9110 defines those shared semantics once, for all versions
Versions differ only in wire encoding and transport
HTTP/1.1 is plaintext and line-oriented, parsed as ASCII

lines: Cookie: sid=9f3a; ab=b   # resent every time

items: One TCP connection carries one in-flight request
Response must finish before the next request starts
A slow 2 MB image stalls every request queued behind it
That is application-level head-of-line blocking

blocks.title: Pipelining Never Saved It
blocks.text: Request 2 could be sent before response 1 arrived, but responses had to return in order, so HOL stayed. Broken proxies mangled it and browsers shipped it disabled.

items: Browsers opened 6 parallel TCP connections per origin
6x handshakes, 6x slow starts, 6x server sockets
Each starts with a ~10 packet (~14 KB) congestion window
Connections compete for bandwidth instead of sharing it
`Cookie`, `User-Agent`, `Accept`, `Referer` repeat in full, uncompressed
Often 500-1500 bytes per request; body may be 0 bytes
100 sub-resources: repeated headers can outweigh the HTML

blocks.title: Latency, Not Bandwidth
blocks.text: Doubling bandwidth barely moves page load; halving RTT nearly halves it. Every HTTP/1.1 workaround is really an attempt to buy back round trips.

blocks.title: Where h2 Came From
items: SPDY (Google, 2009) prototyped it over TLS
Multiplexing plus header compression
Became HTTP/2: RFC 7540 (2015), revised RFC 9113

slides.page_title: Why HTTP/1.1 Ran Out of Road (cont.)

items: Smallest unit is a binary frame, not a line of ASCII
No whitespace guessing, no chunked-encoding text scan
Parsers get simpler and immune to length-ambiguity smuggling
Payload defaults to 16,384 bytes (2^14)
`SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE` negotiates up to 2^24-1
Length field counts payload only, never the 9-byte header
Message = one `HEADERS` frame plus zero or more `DATA` frames
Stream = a bidirectional numbered flow of frames
Memorize: Connection > Streams > Messages > Frames
Client streams odd, server push streams even
IDs strictly increase and are never reused on a connection
Stream 0 is the control stream: `SETTINGS`, `PING`, `GOAWAY`
Connection-level `WINDOW_UPDATE` also rides stream 0

lines: # an HTTP/1.1 server chokes here, early

items: `END_STREAM` flag moves a peer to half-closed
SETTINGS is not a handshake: each side states its own limits
`HEADER_TABLE_SIZE`, `MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS`, `INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE`
`MAX_FRAME_SIZE`, `MAX_HEADER_LIST_SIZE`; every SETTINGS must be ACKed

blocks.title: Cancel Without Closing
items: `RST_STREAM` kills one stream with an error code
HTTP/1.1 could only drop the whole socket
`GOAWAY` names the last stream ID it will process
Clients then know exactly what to retry

blocks.title: How h2 Is Chosen
blocks.text: ALPN in the TLS handshake advertises `h2`. The cleartext `Upgrade: h2c` dance is effectively dead — every browser demands TLS for HTTP/2.

items: Frames from many streams interleave on one connection
Each frame is tagged with its stream ID
Receiver reassembles messages by ID
100 requests can be in flight on a single TCP connection
Requests no longer queue behind a slow response
This kills application-level HOL blocking
Responses may arrive fully out of request order
No positional coupling, unlike pipelining
One TCP handshake, one TLS handshake, one congestion window
That window grows and stays warm across the whole page
Fewer sockets: less server memory, fewer file descriptors
A large win for high-concurrency servers

blocks.title: The Real Parallelism Limit
blocks.text: `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` caps in-flight streams, commonly 100-128. Requests past the cap sit in a client queue, so that number is your true concurrency.

items: One h2 connection may serve several hostnames
Requires the same resolved IP and a certificate SAN match
So `cdn.example.com` and `www.example.com` can share a socket
One changed byte no longer invalidates a giant bundle
Migration rule: enabling h2 without removing hacks yields no speedup

blocks.title: The Bill Comes Later
blocks.text: Everything now rides one TCP connection, which makes that connection a single point of failure for packet loss. Next page develops exactly that.
HOL blocking is the first item in a queue holding up everything behind it, even when the rest could be processed right now. It appears at three independent layers.

items: TCP guarantees one ordered byte stream, nothing more
One lost segment stalls delivery of all later bytes
Including bytes belonging to unrelated h2 streams
The kernel has no idea where stream boundaries are

left.title: h2, 1 conn, 1 loss
items: 10 images multiplexed
all 10 stall
one RTT retransmit

right.title: h1.1, 6 conns
items: 1 conn stalls
5 keep flowing
loss is contained

blocks.title: Yes, h2 Can Be Slower
blocks.text: On lossy networks — poor Wi-Fi, congested mobile — HTTP/2 measurably loses to HTTP/1.1 in real deployments. Not a theoretical footnote.

items: A TLS record cannot be decrypted until fully received
A record spanning 3 packets stalls on any one of them
Mitigate by keeping records at or below one packet
Independent reassembly: each stream has its own buffer
Each stream has its own sequence space too
Loss on stream 3 delays only stream 3
This demands leaving TCP behind, hence UDP
Bursty loss hitting many streams weakens QUIC's edge
Isolated loss is where QUIC shines most
HPACK's shared dynamic table forces ordered header processing
Single-threaded handlers reintroduce blocking above the protocol
CDN terminating h2 but re-fetching over h1.1 blocks the back half

blocks.title: Field Diagnostic
blocks.text: If throughput collapses as loss rate rises but is fine on a clean link, suspect transport HOL blocking before blaming the application.

items: Headers repeat almost identically across requests on one connection
gzip-style compression of headers leaks secrets: the CRIME attack
HPACK (RFC 7541) is purpose-built instead
No LZ77 back-references over attacker-mixable data
Three parts: static table, dynamic table, Huffman coding
Static table: 61 fixed entries, identical on every connection
Per-connection FIFO of header fields already seen
Entry size = name length + value length + 32 bytes overhead
Limit from `SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE`, default 4096 bytes
Oldest entries evicted first when the limit is hit
Indexed: one byte encodes a whole `cookie: <long value>`
Literal with incremental indexing: adds the field to the table
Literal without indexing: used once, not stored
Never-indexed: no intermediary may index it, ever
Huffman: fixed canonical table tuned for header characters
Shaves roughly 30% more off literal strings
The `H` bit in the string-length prefix marks Huffman text
Integers use a prefix plus continuation, so small indexes fit spare bits
Uppercase header names are a protocol error, not a warning
`Connection`, `Keep-Alive`, `Transfer-Encoding`, `Upgrade`, `Proxy-Connection` forbidden
`TE` may carry only `trailers`
Connection management is the framing layer's job now

blocks.title: Split Your Cookies
blocks.text: Multiple cookie-pairs may be sent as separate `cookie` fields, so stable pairs stay indexed while one churning pair does not evict the whole set.

blocks.title: Numbers And Warnings
items: Warm connection: ~1400 bytes of headers down to under 50
Header traffic typically drops 80-90% overall
Never-indexed is the escape hatch for `Authorization`, session cookies
State is per-connection and ordered: a proxy must decode then re-encode
Server sends `PUSH_PROMISE`, reserving an even stream ID
Then sends the response before the client ever asks
Intended for shipping CSS and JS alongside the HTML
Servers cannot know the client's cache, so pushes are often wasted bytes
Wasted pushes compete with the HTML for bandwidth
Chrome removed HTTP/2 push in 2022
HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) omits push in practice; the ecosystem moved on

slides.page_title: Server Push, Priority, and Flow Control

items: RFC 7540: dependency tree, parent stream IDs, weights 1-256
Plus exclusive-dependency reparenting — overcomplicated
Implemented inconsistently and commonly ignored by servers
RFC 9113 deprecated the whole scheme

lines: # u=5, i for a below-fold image, incremental

items: On one shared connection, ordering decides first paint
Render-blocking CSS must beat below-the-fold images
Otherwise multiplexing actively hurts perceived speed

left.title: h1.1 sequential
items: one at a time
each finishes fast
CSS usable early

right.title: naive round-robin
items: all progress equally
all finish at the end
worst for rendering
Credit-based and receiver-driven: the receiver advertises bytes it accepts
Applied per-stream and per-connection independently
`WINDOW_UPDATE` frames grant more credit
Default initial window is 65,535 bytes
Applies to `DATA` frames only, never `HEADERS`

blocks.title: The 5 Mbps Ceiling
blocks.text: A 64 KB window over a 100 ms RTT caps one stream near 5 Mbps no matter how fat the link is. Raise `INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE` on high-BDP paths.

items: Flow control also lets a client throttle a paused video stream
It does that without killing the connection or the other streams

slides.page_title: Server Push, Priority, and Flow Control (cont.)

blocks.title: Two Real DoS Bugs
items: `CONTINUATION` carries header blocks too big for one frame
CONTINUATION flood (CVE-2024-27316-class): unbounded, uncounted frames
Rapid Reset (CVE-2023-44487): open then instantly `RST_STREAM`
Beat `MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` in work terms; fix is counting and rate-limiting resets

blocks.text: A Transport, Not A Protocol Version

items: QUIC (RFC 9000) is general-purpose, connection-oriented, encrypted, multiplexed
It rides on top of UDP; HTTP/3 is just one application of it
Middleboxes drop unknown IP protocols, so a new one was impossible
Ossification made TCP unevolvable; QUIC hides inside UDP datagrams
It lives in userspace, shipping with an app release, not a kernel upgrade
Integrated, not layered: no separate TLS record layer exists
The handshake travels in QUIC `CRYPTO` frames

blocks.title: 0-RTT Is Replayable
blocks.text: An attacker can replay 0-RTT data, so restrict it to idempotent requests — a plain `GET` with no side effects, never a `POST` that charges a card.

items: Nearly the whole packet is encrypted and authenticated, header included
Only a few bits and the connection ID stay visible to the network
Header protection additionally masks the packet number
Middleboxes cannot track or rewrite QUIC internals — deliberate anti-ossification
Connection ID replaces the 4-tuple as connection identity
So the connection survives an IP or port change
Wi-Fi to cellular keeps the same connection and its congestion state
No re-handshake, no dropped video call

slides.page_title: QUIC: A New Transport on UDP

items: Each stream has its own flow control and its own offset space
That allows independent reassembly, killing transport HOL blocking
Frame types: `STREAM`, `ACK`, `CRYPTO`, `MAX_DATA`
Plus `NEW_CONNECTION_ID`, `PATH_CHALLENGE`, `CONNECTION_CLOSE`

blocks.title: Better Than TCP At Loss
items: Packet numbers never repeat, even on retransmission
So TCP's retransmission ambiguity disappears; RTT samples are exact
ACK ranges plus explicit ACK delay sharpen the estimate
Congestion control is pluggable: NewReno per RFC 9002, often BBR or CUBIC

blocks.title: Amplification Defense
blocks.text: A server must not send more than 3x the bytes received from an unvalidated client address, which shuts down QUIC reflection attacks.

items: HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) maps HTTP semantics onto QUIC
Same methods, status codes, headers; no reliance on TCP
QUIC owns streams, reliability, flow control, congestion control
So HTTP/3's own framing layer is far thinner than HTTP/2's
One request/response pair = exactly one QUIC bidirectional stream
HTTP/3 does not implement multiplexing, it inherits it
Unidirectional streams carry control data
One control stream per side, plus QPACK encoder and decoder streams
A stream type byte identifies each one

caption.text: Your page is slow because of round trips, not bandwidth — and every HTTP/1.1 trick you learned (sharding, spriting, base64 inlining) now actively fights HTTP/2. 10 pages of study notes on binary framing, HPACK vs QPACK, the three layers of head-of-line blocking, and why QUIC had to hide inside UDP to survive the middleboxes. Save it for the next time someone says "just turn on h3".
